text.p: H.F. Ahmanson and Co's revised bid for Great Western Financial Corp puts pressure on Washington Mutual Savings Inc to follow suit.
Industry analysts said Ahmanson's latest offer, which provides a premium in excess of $400 million over white knight Washington Mutual's agreement, is more attractive.
"On a per dollar basis, it's a more attractive bid at this point and I imagine the onus is on Washington Mutual to make an improved offer," said Leslie Nelkin, analyst with Furhman Selz.

Ahmanson, which originally offered to exchange 1.05 of its shares for each Great Western share, now will pay between 1.1 and 1.2 of its shares, depending on the price of Ahmanson's stock when the deal closes.
Great Western said its board would study the revised bid. Washington Mutual said it had no plans to raise its bid and believes its deal, to exchange 0.9 shares, would prevail.

Ahmanson also projected $100 million in additional merger benefits from the deal, which was considered a big plus by some analysts who believe that Washington Mutual's projections have been overly optimistic.
"While Ahmanson has added revenue enhancements, its original assumptions are still reasonable," said Nelkin.

Ahmanson executives said many of its newest assumptions were based on information released during Washington Mutual's presentations. Washington Mutual plans to meet with investors this week to outline its deal.

Many analysts preferred Ahmanson's offer due to its greater overlap with Great Western, which provides more cost savings. But other analysts said they had a lot of confidence in the ability of Washington Mutual to execute on its promises due to the company's proven track record with acquisitions.
"The economics are behind Ahmanson, but there is clearly a perception that Washington Mutual can do the better execution," said Charlotte Chamberlain of Jefferies and Co.

Todd Pitsinger of Friedman Billings and Ramsey said Ahmanson's bid forces Great Western at the very least to talk with Ahmanson. "They can't merely dismiss Ahmanson's bid as they had in the past," he said.
"Ahmanson is essentially capitalizing on the terminology of the definitive Washington Mutual/Great Western agreement which forces Great Western to look at a competitive bid," said Pitsinger.
Under Washington Mutual's agreement, Great Western has agreed to pay a breakup fee of as much as $175 million to Washington Mutual if the deal falls through.
Ahmanson has said it if succeeds, it will return the breakup fees to shareholders.
